items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: This was through the Peter Duchin office.

ctx.x: I guess it makes you appreciate, to pay those kind of dues makes the good times that much better.

That’s true too in a sense. And it also makes you aware of treating other people fairly yourself. And if you ever find yourself in that position, the first thing I think about is treating the other guys the same way. I’ve done recordings and things like that, or I did something for Schaefer Beer, oh I guess a couple of years ago, and I was the leader of this particular group. And so rather than take — they say we’ll pay you a certain amount of money. This was through the Peter Duchin office. And I accepted it, I…
It’s a good lesson. I remember you talking a little bit about some fellows who would try to cut corners and play the game of booking two sessions at the same time too, and that kind of —

items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We have a certain routine, because the repertoire that he plays are the things that people dance to, and he plays them in a certain order.

ctx.x: I think in terms of my questions that they gave me and the questions that I had – ah, one last thing. I wanted to ask you a bit about what you’ve been doing the past couple of years. I know you’ve been playing with both Dick Hyman and with Peter Duchin. I wanted to ask you about what those experiences are like.

With Peter Duchin, it’s pretty cut and dry. We do basically the same things wherever we go. We have a certain routine, because the repertoire that he plays are the things that people dance to, and he plays them in a certain order. Sometimes he plays requests.
So it’s almost like playing a Broadway show, where you do one thing. You’ve got the order down.
